articles.title: With layered pigments, a painter builds imagined mountains
articles.author: Brangien Davis
paras: When Camas Logue was a kid, he told his grandmother he was planning to be an artist, a doctor and the pope. “She was Catholic,” he says with a laugh, “so I think maybe I was trying to impress her.”

He ended up being right about one out of three. A painter, wood carver, basket weaver and printmaker, Logue is also a drummer in the band Black Belt Eagle Scout. With this multidisciplinary multitude of options, our Art by Northwest profile focuses on Logue’s paintings. ( Stream the episode now , or watch the broadcast premiere on Cascade PBS, tonight at 8:50 p.m.)

I first spotted Logue’s work in the 2025 group show Through the Light: The Sublime in Contemporary Northwest Art at the Museum of Northwest Art in La Conner. I was immediately drawn into his mysterious and richly hued landscapes — craggy land formations in shades of pink-red, highlighter yellow and periwinkle blue, often iced with drips of snow white. Some looked like extraterrestrial snapshots, others like surreal vistas from a dream.

An enrolled member of the Klamath Tribes in Oregon, Logue was born and raised in Portland, where his artist grandmother sparked his creative aspirations. His first foray into landscape art involved carving scrimshaw drawings onto vintage piano keys — scritchy sketches of natural places he’d explored in the Northwest. In 2020, he moved to the Swinomish Indian Tribal Community, the homeland of his wife, Black Belt Eagle Scout singer/songwriter Katherine Paul.

Just as each track of a song builds depth and resonance, Logue uses a process of layering to bring his remembered places to life in visual art. Putting paint upon pigment, lines over landscapes, he imbues each piece with an experiential truth, rather than reaching for a precise depiction of terrain.

“What I’m going for with my paintings is trying to replicate the energy or the momentum of what’s happening in that place,” Logue explains in the episode. Sometimes the emotional punch lies in a single line of paint, which he allows to drip down the canvas and direct the flow of the work.

Toward the end of his layering process Logue returns to the scrimshaw skills he plied on piano keys long ago, this time using graphite to scratch tiny lines across the surface of the painting. Using this meticulous method, he highlights and defines strata both geologic and poetic — as if to etch a memory of place in his mind.

With the launch of Art by Northwest Season 3 we’re developing quite a cohort of innovative regional artists. I’m always keeping up with past and forthcoming artists featured on the show, and will keep you posted on their new work and new shows in upcoming newsletters.

Work by two of our previously featured artists is currently on view in a terrific group show at the Bainbridge Island Museum of Art. Co-curated by Robin Little Wing Sigo, Indigenous Craft (through Nov. 1) showcases work by 20+ prominent Indigenous artists from around the Salish Sea.

Among them is carver Jennifer Angaiak Wood ( profiled in Season 2 ), who creates masks based on Yup’ik stories from her heritage. Wood emphasizes that while her masks use traditional techniques, her materials and approach are deliberately contemporary.

Also in the mix at BIMA is prolific artist Joe Feddersen ( another Season 2 alum ), of the Colville Confederated Tribes. Look for his intricately woven waxed-linen baskets adorned with curious characters, such as aliens, dog-headed humans and parking lots.

And if you’re anywhere near Missoula, Montana, this fall, absolutely do not miss Feddersen’s retrospective, Earth, Water, Sky (Sept. 4 - Dec. 1) at the Missoula Museum of Art. This expansive show, previously staged at the Northwest Museum of Arts and Culture in Spokane, includes Feddersen’s etched glass vessels, fused glass curtains, prints, baskets and more.

Lastly, an opportunity for a sneak peek of sorts. Blacksmith Maria Cristalli will be featured in Episode 3 of Art by Northwest (coming Sept. 3), but if you hurry you can see her remarkable work in person at Gray Sky Gallery in Pioneer Square. Wrought and Woven (through Aug. 31) features Cristalli’s hefty forged steel sculptures, inspired by the forested (and burned) surroundings at her Cle Elum home.

Watch Art by Northwest Season 3, Episode 2, profiling Camas Logue , and stay tuned for six more new artist profiles from across the region. While you wait, catch up on past episodes of Art by Northwest , nominated for two Northwest Regional Emmy Awards.

articles.title: ‘I fight pain and fear with art’: how Yayoi Kusama blazed a trail for neurodivergent artists
articles.author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
paras: The pioneering Japanese artist talked openly about how her mental health and neurodivergence informed her creativity, paving the way for the likes of Turner prize winner Nnena Kalu

Yayoi Kusama – who has died at the age of 97 – was 10 when she first started experiencing vivid hallucinations consisting of visual and aural disturbances, which she described as “flashes of light, auras, or dense fields of dots”. A drawing from 1939, of a woman in a kimono assumed to be her mother, shows her obliterated by those dots; they would become Kusama’s artistic obsession. She hallucinated flowers, too. “I was looking at the red flower patterns of the tablecloth on a table, and when I looked up I saw the same pattern covering the ceiling, the windows and the walls, and finally all over the room, my body and the universe”, she once said, when asked about that recurring motif. “I felt as if I had begun to self-obliterate, to revolve in the infinity of endless time and the absoluteness of space, and be reduced to nothingness.”

For Kusama, art making was a means of survival. “I fight pain, anxiety, and fear every day, and the only method I have found that relieved my illness is to keep creating art. I followed the thread of art and somehow discovered a path that would allow me to live”, she said in a 2012 interview . In so doing, she became one of the most acclaimed and admired contemporary artists, staging happenings and influencing the pop art movement as a pioneering figure in the New York avant garde. Her exhibitions and major retrospectives draw huge crowds. In 2022, due to enormous public demand, Tate Modern in London extended her Infinity Mirror Rooms show for a whole extra year (it ended up running until 2024).

articles.title: Dolly Parton was more than a musical idol – for some fans, she was a spiritual icon
articles.author:
<name>Sarah Dees, Associate Professor of American Religions, Iowa State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/sarah-dees-862831"/>
paras: As soon as news broke about the death of beloved songwriter Dolly Parton, I began receiving condolence messages from across the country, and around the world.

They came from friends, family and colleagues who knew I’d been working on a biography of the country legend – everyone from a conservative Catholic monk to advocates for queer and trans rights. The list reflects the even more diverse array of fans, people from countless backgrounds, who are mourning her loss.

The main focus of my project is Parton’s own spirituality, starting with her Appalachian upbringing. But it also examines her fandoms, including some people who elevate the singer to an almost sacred status. This was the case before her death – and even more so now.

As a scholar of American religions , I teach my students about practices, texts and beliefs that many of them immediately consider “religious” – for example, a worship service led by a pastor. However, religion is also found far beyond these official times and spaces , including in popular culture. According to scholar America Wolff , fandoms resemble religious groups in the way they focus on a single popular figure who inspires systems of belief, ritual and law.

Looking at Parton’s life reveals how a celebrity can incorporate religion into their public persona, without ostracizing admirers from other traditions. She discussed religion in interviews throughout her career, as well as in her 1994 memoir , where she recounted her maternal grandfather, a fundamentalist pastor, preaching hellfire and brimstone.

In 1971, for example, she told journalist Gene Guerrero how religion inspired some of her songs : “My mama used to read us all the Bible stories. I know the Bible pretty well, and I especially loved the stories.” That same year, she released “ The Golden Streets of Glory ,” the first of her several gospel albums.

Six years later, talking with Rolling Stone interviewer Chet Flippo , Parton claimed that she wasn’t a Christian. But “I do believe, I know there is a God and He is still the best friend I got in the world,” she explained. “I talk to Him often, but I’m one of the world’s sinners.”

Later in her life, though, Parton embraced the label “Christian” – albeit in a way that was very much her own. In the memoir “My Life and Other Unfinished Business,” she explained that “Christianity and its symbols are powerful parts of my life.” However, she diverged from socially conservative elements of her grandfather’s faith by embracing makeup and flashy fashion, celebrating her own sexuality, and speaking up for LGBTQ+ rights .

She was never interested in proselytizing. People do not have to embrace Christianity “to be a decent and worthwhile human being,” she wrote. “Spirituality is the most intimate part of a person’s makeup, and it’s strictly up to the individual to choose how to express it.”

This openness explains part of Parton’s widespread appeal. The popular podcast “ Dolly Parton’s America ,” produced by journalists Jad Abumrad and Shima Oliaee , was based on the premise that Parton is one of the few public figures to have fans across the political spectrum.

After her death, President Donald Trump posted a tribute on his social media site, TruthSocial, and ordered that flags be flown at half-staff for a week. At the same time, in the Castro neighborhood of San Francisco – a haven for the queer community – a Pride flag was also flying at half-staff in her honor .

Mourners include Jesuit priest and author James J. Martin, who thanked Parton for “ teaching me about the Christian life ,” and numerous Christian musicians who looked up to her. “She was the epitome of faith, grace, talent, beauty and humour,” country artist Carrie Underwood wrote . “She had a humble heart for Jesus and made everyone around her feel special.”
But even non-Christians discussed Parton in sacred terms: a “ secular American saint ,” as Vox writer Constance Grady designated her in 2021.

Beyond her music, these fans admired her philanthropy, from the Imagination Library program that distributes books to children around the world to her US$1 million donation that helped fund COVID-19 vaccine research . They also highlighted her support for the Black Lives Matter movement and LGBTQ+ rights . “Dolly Parton is beloved because she has devoted her career to standing for love,” Grady wrote .

Even before her death, though, some people idolized her in a saint-like way. In 2011, for example, photographer Alice Hawkins produced a project titled “ Dolly Parton is my religon .” Rev. Lindy Vogado, a Presbyterian pastor, likened her to a prophet . “Dolly Parton, through her life and work, inspires us to be better versions of ourselves,” Vogado wrote in 2025. “Just like any good prophet would do.”

In recent years, churches in Illinois , Oklahoma and New York have held services based on “the gospel of Dolly.” I attended the service in New York, which interspersed Parton’s songs with readings from scripture and homilies. Like the other services, the one I attended emphasized Parton’s “teachings”: love, care and acceptance.

Since her death, the religious language has only intensified. Musician Roseanne Cash referred to the singer as a “goddess ” on Instagram, and cartoonist Marshall Ramsey portrayed her as an angel . “Listen, I’m fairly well atheist and have been for decades,” Threads user @cartergoesplaces proclaimed , “but Dolly Parton is in heaven with Jesus now. That’s simply a fact, and I’ll hear no arguments, no matter how vast the cosmos…”

Parton had her own personal brand of Christian religiosity, but she encouraged others to find and follow their own paths. I believe this helps to explain the huge outpouring of admiration – from followers of many religious traditions, followers of none, and followers of Dolly herself.

Sarah Dees does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Galápagos corals show El Niño events are more extreme now than in past 1,000 years – here’s how my team made the discovery
articles.author:
<name>Julia Cole, Professor of Earth and Environmental Science, University of Michigan</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/julia-cole-2051230"/>
paras: Temperatures have warmed dramatically across the equatorial Pacific Ocean in 2026, signaling the onset of a strong and potentially historic El Niño . These events can affect weather around the world, and the intensity of recent El Niño events is raising alarm that, as global temperatures rise , they are becoming stronger and more destructive .

To understand how these climate patterns are changing, we need to understand what happened during El Niño events in the past, but observations go back only a few decades. So, my colleagues and I went to the Galápagos Islands – at the heart of the El Niño pattern – to find answers from some of nature’s best record keepers: corals.

In records preserved by living and ancient fossil corals, we found that, on average, El Niño events have been stronger in the past 40 years than at any time in the past millennium, with higher temperatures that lead to more powerful effects on weather.
That intensification also coincides with human-caused global warming.

Our results, just published in the journal Science, suggest that the 1982-83 and 1997-98 El Niños – two of the strongest in recent memory – may be harbingers of more extreme events to come as the planet warms.

One of the strongest El Niños hit in 1982, with devastating consequences for the Galápagos Islands. It triggered a marine heat wave that reverberated through one of the most distinctive and unspoiled ecosystems on the planet.

Exceptionally warm surface water blocked the usual upwelling of cool, nutrient-rich water that fuels the food chain for marine life. The result ravaged communities that rely on the ocean – fish, birds, marine mammals, and people who fish for their livelihoods throughout the eastern tropical Pacific. In the extraordinary heat, more than 95% of Galápagos corals died .

The heat wave was caused by an exceptionally strong El Niño event, part of a climate pattern that begins in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, around the Galápagos Islands, as the trade winds shift. El Niño’s warm ocean water alters the atmospheric circulation above, diverting storm tracks and changing patterns of floods, droughts and tropical storms around the globe.

The 1982-83 El Niño contributed to climate extremes worldwide , from flooding in Kenya and Peru to drought in Indonesia and Brazil, costing the global economy as much as US$4 trillion by some estimates. A similarly strong El Niño in 1997-98 resulted in 23,000 deaths from disease and climate disasters.
But we wanted to know: Are such powerful El Niño events unusual in the context of history?

Even in 1983, scientists were surprised to find that such a strong event had been underway. Historical records of El Niño are sparse before the era of satellite observations. Fortunately, long-lived corals growing in the tropical Pacific can provide a history of El Niño that extends our view into the past.

As corals grow, they preserve a record of local ocean temperatures over time. In the Galápagos, because of their location, that record reveals the history of El Niño events and of their cooler counterpart, La Niña.

Like trees that produce annual growth rings, corals add skeletal layers of calcium carbonate year after year. The alternating bands of higher and lower density reveal changes in the coral’s growth rate during each year and can serve as a timekeeper. The history of the ocean temperature is embedded in the chemical composition of the skeleton itself.

To track the history of water temperatures, we measured two chemical parameters – the ratio of heavy to light oxygen isotopes and the ratio of strontium to calcium – both of which reflect the seawater temperature in which the coral grew.
In the Galápagos, because of the islands’ location, the sea surface temperature swings between warm El Niño years and colder La Niña years, when upwelling of nutrients is stronger.

The largest living corals in the Galápagos grow in the northern islands of Wolf and Darwin, in water 20 to 50 feet deep. To study their history , we dived down and took core samples from long-lived corals, some 8 to 10 feet tall.

Every core we drilled from a living coral showed evidence in its calcified skeleton that the coral had suffered during the 1982-83 El Niño event. We saw obvious “death horizons” – dense layers of calcified material produced by other reef organisms such as algae, gastropods and barnacles interrupting the lattice of the skeleton .

We also took samples of fossil corals around the archipelago – mostly dead coral boulders found along the islands’ shorelines. Radiometric dating told us that these fossil corals were up to 4,500 years old. Those samples provide an even deeper view of El Niño’s history.

Back in the lab, we sliced the coral cores lengthwise into slabs and used a drill to extract powdered samples, each representing about one month’s growth, along a path from youngest to oldest. We analyzed the geochemistry of each sample. In the chemical ratios from thousands of samples, we found seasonal cycles spanning many decades and exceptional warm and cold years that revealed a unique history of El Niño and La Niña events.
Our data show clearly that the strength of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation has intensified as global temperatures have warmed.
The chemistry of the corals revealed that El Niño events from the past 40 years were stronger than at any other time sampled in the past millennium.

The coral data aligns with ocean temperatures measured from thermometers over the past century. But the coral records extend much further back in time, providing long-term context to show that modern El Niño events are more extreme than before the industrial era began.

The El Niño intensification we observed, starting in the mid- to late 20th century, is also greater than what nearly all climate models suggest would result from natural causes. It appears to be closely connected to human-caused global warming – a conclusion in line with expectations from most climate models .

Not all models anticipate El Niños strengthening as the climate warms, but our data shows that unusual strengthening has accompanied recent warming – an association that may allow scientists to identify models that most closely track observations.
A stronger El Niño-Southern Oscillation means more intense and damaging climate extremes across the globe. If humanity can anticipate those hazards, we can prepare and perhaps avoid the worst damage.

Fortunately, scientists understand enough about El Niño and La Niña events today to be able to forecast them up to a year in advance . But such predictions depend on continuous, careful climate measurements from satellites and buoys across the remote tropical Pacific , coupled with continuous improvements in climate modeling and forecasting capabilities.
Those capabilities are now more important than ever as global warming accelerates.
Julia Cole receives funding from the US National Science Foundation.

articles.title: US-Canada trade war deepens as Trump revives Depression-era trade tool – what’s at stake for consumers and the midterms
articles.author:
<name>Kent Jones, Professor Emeritus of Economics, Babson College</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/kent-jones-2543311"/>
paras: The United States and Canada, historically close allies, are moving further into a full-blown trade war with no end in sight.

On Aug. 25, 2026, Canada imposed tariffs of up to 50% on hundreds of U.S. goods after the U.S. placed similar, long-threatened levies on Canadian products. It followed the collapse of trade talks that had been inching towards a deal.

The next day, U.S. President Donald Trump called Canada “one of the worst countries in the world to deal with.” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney claimed Trump was trying to “destroy” his country’s auto industry. Only a few days earlier a deal was reportedly very close .

One of the most notable aspects of the collapse in trade negotiations lies in Trump’s unprecedented use of an untested tool in the Tariff Act of 1930 , otherwise known as the Smoot-Hawley tariffs. Economists generally agree that the act’s escalating retaliatory tariffs extended the Great Depression by sparking a global trade war. Amplified by foreign retaliation and falling global gross domestic product, U.S. trade fell by two-thirds from 1929-1932.

Smoot-Hawley contains a provision known as Section 338, which provides an additional feature: The president may, on his own authority, impose unilateral tariffs of 50% if a foreign country’s policies “discriminated” against the United States.

But the section was never invoked, as the damage from the other Smoot-Hawley tariffs was already done. That is, until July 2026 , when Trump first threatened the 50% tariffs on Canada for its “discriminatory treatment” of U.S. products.
As an economist who has studied trade policy for 49 years, I can explain how the two countries got embroiled in a trade war and what it means for U.S. consumers, companies and the midterms.
Both sides are finger-pointing at the other over what caused the proposed deal to fall apart during the final days of the trade negotiations.
The Canadians were interested primarily in reducing high U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos. They claimed they had a preliminary deal to lower steel and aluminum tariffs from 50% to 25%.

In the late stages of the negotiations, however, U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was apparently lobbied heavily by U.S. steel and aluminum producers to hold the line on these tariffs. Lutnick was also against reductions in the U.S. auto and truck tariffs and allegedly withdrew whatever reductions were on the table.
As a result, other parts of the deal started to unwind as well.

The Canadians had offered to reopen the Keystone oil pipeline deal that had been canceled by President Joe Biden in 2021. But once the deal on lower steel, aluminum and auto tariffs was nixed, Canada pulled the Keystone deal off the table as well.
The U.S. had also demanded that Canada reverse the Canadian provinces’ removal of U.S. liquor off their store shelves. Sales of U.S. booze in Canada have plunged as a result.
But the lack of progress on the major metal and auto tariffs, combined with a backlash from the Canadian provinces themselves, forced that concession off the table as well.
Canada is a major supplier of goods to the U.S. , exporting about US$451 billion in 2025 – ranking second after Mexico.

As soon as talks broke off, the Trump administration followed through on earlier threats to impose a 50% tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian exports, including auto parts, forestry products, furniture, textiles, whiskey and hockey equipment, under Section 338 of Smoot-Hawley.
That’s about 4% of Canada’s exports to the United States.

Canada’s Carney responded with his own already prepared list of $20 billion in U.S. imports to face tariffs of up to 50%, targeting products that he surely bets will anger voters in swing states heading into the midterm elections.
Examples include Wisconsin cheese, Maine seafood and Kentucky washers and dryers – GE Appliances is headquartered in Louisville, Kentucky.
Tensions between Canada and the U.S. and have been high ever since Trump returned to office.
He has continually complained about Canada “ ripping us off ” and being “ among the worst countries ” in the world to deal with.
And he has repeatedly threatened to make Canada the 51st state, an issue that has particularly angered Canadians and served to unite public opinion across the political spectrum against Trump.

For Carney, a critical sticking point was the late addition by U.S. negotiators requiring Canadian trade policy to align permanently with U.S. interests. Carney viewed this demand as a transfer of Canadian sovereignty to the U.S., a step toward making Canada “the 51st state.”
So all in all, perhaps it’s not so surprising that a near deal would collapse into a trade war.

In addition, Canada has been unusual in standing up to Trump in this way. The only other country to do that is China, and it’s risky for a smaller country like Canada to retaliate in this way. But Canadians are pretty united in their unfavorable views of Trump , so Carney has a strong domestic position to stand up to him.

The 50% tariffs Trump unilaterally imposed on Canada apply to goods that had previously been exempt from most other tariffs due to the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement , which replaced NAFTA in 2020.

Since tariffs are a tax on the purchaser, U.S. consumers and companies will have to pay 50% more to buy the products subject to the tariffs. Many of the Canadian imports are concentrated in U.S. border states such as Maine, New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio and Wisconsin. Another border state, Michigan, is closely tied to automobile production with the Canadian province of Ontario.
In many cases, Canada’s retaliatory tariffs will be felt most strongly in states where Trump’s Republican Party stands to be affected by reductions in U.S. exports that will result from the levies.

The political backlash against Trump’s tariffs in the U.S. doesn’t appear to be deterring him from imposing more of them, even as the impact of midterm elections hinges on results in several swing states along the Canadian border.

While the total impact on overall U.S. prices may not be large, the combination of U.S. and Canadian tariffs together could be significant for products that are heavily traded between the two countries, such as Michigan auto parts and New England seafood, as well as in U.S. regions where Canadian market shares are large. U.S farmers and manufacturers may also lose sales to Canada.

If Trump’s tariffs remain in place and U.S. importers can no longer absorb the tariff costs and remain profitable, U.S. prices are likely to continue to rise as importers require consumers to pay a larger share of the tariffs. It’s probably unwise to predict what Trump will do with tariffs between now and the midterms or now and the end of his term in 2028. A victorious Democratic Party in charge of the House and Senate could change the political landscape considerably.

It’s worth noting that the global trading system that emerged in 1947, from the ashes of war, depression and tit-for-tat trade battles, was purposely designed to eliminate trade wars , since they typically make us all worse off. And the trade liberalization that followed worked, delivering enormous wealth to the U.S. and the world economy in the years since.
I believe it would be a shame if we returned to those days, and the unfortunate economic consequences that came with them.

articles.title: Why the US-Canada trade war could change how American farmers grow their crops for years
articles.author:
<name>Jayash Paudel, Associate Professor of Economics, University of Oklahoma</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jayash-paudel-2610171"/>
paras: U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada is getting personal for American farmers.

After trade talks between the two longtime allies fell apart in mid-August 2026, Trump imposed 50% tariffs on a wide range of Canadian imports worth roughly US$20 billion (CAD$27 billion). Canada responded on Aug. 25, 2026, by announcing its own plan to put retaliatory tariffs of 15% to 50% on the same value of U.S. goods, effective Sept. 8.
Canada’s list includes dairy products and agricultural equipment, and there is an unspoken threat that it could expand to a crucial component in fertilizer that U.S. farmers rely on.
I have studied agriculture and water quality for more than a decade, including whether trade rules change how farmers manage their land.

In my assessment, the enduring effect of this trade war on U.S. agriculture, if it continues to escalate, won’t be a single bad season. Across thousands of farms, farmers may have to reduce their fertilizer use as prices – already high from supply disruptions because of the war in Iran – rise. It may have little visible consequence at first, but the lasting impact could emerge later in smaller future harvests if this trade war continues.
Canada’s tariffs aren’t directly aimed at farmers, but farms will feel the cost if they go into effect.

A tariff is a tax on imported goods paid by the importer, effectively raising the cost of those goods. When China responded to U.S. tariffs during the first Trump administration in 2018, its retaliatory tariffs hit U.S. soybeans and automobiles, directly affecting the American agricultural sector. Research shows U.S. agricultural exports to China fell by $7 billion to $10 billion a year, as Chinese buyers shifted to Brazilian suppliers.
Canada’s tariff list for Sept. 8 appears to match U.S. tariffs dollar for dollar. I believe agriculture is caught in the broader fallout, not directly targeted.
However, the effect will still reach farms.

Canada is one of the largest markets for American food, importing about $28 billion in U.S. agricultural products in 2025. Both U.S. and Canada are also deeply integrated in agricultural trade and farm equipment markets. Farm equipment is assembled from parts that cross the border. Live cattle and processed foods also move both ways.
Tariffs can raise costs along that chain. Canadian officials, recognizing that, included several billion dollars in aid for their farmers in announcing the tariff plan.

An analysis of the tariffs Trump ordered in 2025 on countries around the world shows how fast agricultural trade flows reorganize under this sort of pressure. When North American trade barriers go up, U.S. imports of fruits and vegetables from Canada and Mexico typically drop, with buyers turning to Australia and Argentina instead. The result is often higher consumer prices for key agriculture products in the United States.
Canada is also a major source of potash , a fertilizer ingredient that U.S. farmers depend on.

If pushed too far, Canada could levy export tariffs on potash and, potentially, even on oil, natural gas and electricity, raising the price for U.S. buyers. The widespread impact that such a move would have on U.S. consumer prices may give Canada leverage going forward.

Crops require three main nutrients: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Potassium comes almost entirely from potash . American mines produce less than 1% of the global potash supply, and the U.S. imports more than 80% of its potassium from the Elk Point Basin in Saskatchewan, Canada. These are geology-based U.S. constraints in agriculture.
Notably, potash was not included in the U.S. tariff list. Taxing such a key agricultural input would have raised costs for American growers.
American farmers are already squeezed on fertilizer costs.

When the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran shut down shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, it cut off a large source of nitrogen fertilizer, raising fertilizer and fuel prices. A Farm Bureau survey in April 2026 found 70% of farmers said they couldn’t afford all the fertilizer they needed during spring planting.

Nitrogen washes out of soil and must be reapplied every year. Potassium and phosphorus, on the other hand, build up as a reserve. This means that a farmer facing high prices can skip an application and briefly live off that reserve. This is consistent with advice from agricultural extension researchers who compare this coping strategy to a fuel gauge: You can make a trip or two without refilling, but not the third.
Potash was the one major nutrient that the Iran shock didn’t directly affect. However, if Canada raises the price of potash, that could have similar effects .

When fertilizer prices spike, farmers tend to cut phosphorus and potassium first and nitrogen last. But restoring potassium in soil takes time , with several pounds of fertilizer for every pound of soil-test potassium recovered, spread over years. So, even a one-year restriction on potash access can have an impact.

Economic research shows that trade policy uncertainty affects agricultural decisions even before tariffs take effect. A farmer who cannot predict next year’s costs may delay the purchase and hope that prices will ease.
Fertilizer is often bought months ahead of planting, so hesitating in the fall can mean less goes on the ground in the spring. Uncertainty alone can reduce what gets applied before any tariff exists.

If U.S. farmers end up facing higher prices or short supplies for potassium fertilizer, the effects over time, including the chance of smaller yields, would arrive at the grocery store in the form of higher food prices long after the tariffs are likely to be lifted.

Jayash Paudel currently receives funding from the US Department of Agriculture and the National Science Foundation, and his previous research has received funding from the Institute for Humane Studies, the World Institute for Development Economics Research, and Data Institute for Societal Challenges.

articles.title: Why Democrats are amplifying corruption talk: A historical strategy for parties out of power
articles.author:
<name>Robert Boatright, Professor of Political Science, Clark University; Institute for Humane Studies</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/robert-boatright-273088"/>
paras: If you have seen campaign ads for the midterm elections, you have likely noticed that a major theme this year is corruption.

New Hampshire congressman and Senate candidate Chris Pappas has framed his campaign around his anti-corruption efforts in Congress, claiming that his anti-corruption record includes the fact that he “doesn’t take a dime of corporate PAC money,” opposes congressional stock trading, and wants to ban companies from using AI to set prices based on Americans’ personal data.

A super PAC allied with Pappas’ prospective Republican opponent , John Sununu, has run ads calling Pappas corrupt, alleging that Pappas “serves on a House committee that oversees Uber, where his husband, a former lobbyist, serves in an executive policy role.”

This is one of many races where corruption has a prime role. On her DCinbox Substack , which tracks “how members of Congress communicate with constituents,” Lindsey Cormack shows that Democrats this year are talking about corruption six times as much as they did in 2022 and four times as much as Republicans have this year in their emails to constituents. This suggests that the corruption talk is a part of Democratic Party strategy.

One possibility might be that there is a lot of corruption happening . Yet a puzzling feature of these advertisements is that few of them mention President Donald Trump, despite plentiful allegations of corrupt acts by Trump and members of his administration.

Another might be that the public is particularly concerned about corruption. Research shows, however, that the public is always a little bit concerned about corruption , and that these worries often do not correspond with particular actions by politicians.
The talk, it turns out, is not really about specific, identifiable corruption. It’s about delegitimizing your opponent.

My recent book, “ American Corruption Talk ,” co-authored with Molly Brigid McGrath, analyzes the prevalence of what we call “corruption talk” by presidents and presidential candidates since the nation’s founding. We argue that corruption talk is different from talk about real corruption – many Americans identify things as being corrupt even when they do not meet the textbook definition of corruption.
In our book, we identify three types of corruption:
• Transactional corruption is inherent in particular acts – offering or accepting a bribe, for instance.
• Moral corruption is being a rotten person – someone who is corrupt is not trustworthy, even if we cannot identify anything specific that person has done wrong.
• Systemic corruption has to do with the government’s behavior itself. It is not a matter of bad people but bad institutions.
Corruption talk blurs the distinctions between these three distinct things.
In the book, we explore changes over time in how presidents, presidential candidates and party platforms discuss corruption.

We found that parties out of power talk much more about corruption than those who are in power. Corruption talk is popular among politicians who want to avoid taking strong ideological positions or tying themselves closely to their party leaders. They can use it as evidence of bipartisanship , as a way to say they are not career politicians , or to emphasize their competence and integrity .
Corruption is what political scientists call a valence issue – almost everyone thinks corruption is bad, but not everyone agrees about how much of it there is.

Corruption talk, it turns out, is useful for bringing together parties or candidates who want to avoid talking about divisive issues. It is also a way to delegitimize the opposition. If one’s opponents are corrupt, it doesn’t matter what they say. They’re the kind of people who would do corrupt things, even if they haven’t done them yet.
The Democrats’ corruption talk of 2026 checks all of these boxes.
Democrats have internal divisions, from political ideology to policy on Israel , which they may wish to avoid talking about.

Talking about things Trump has done requires too much explanation – it’s hard to describe the Constitution’s foreign emoluments clause in a 30-second ad. That clause bars the president from accepting “‘any present, Emolument, Office, or Title, of any kind whatever’ from a foreign government unless Congress consents ,” and Trump has been accused of violating it .
But talking about corruption in a moral or systemic sense – observing that the country is in decline, or that elites are out of touch – can be effective.

“To every Utahn tired of chaos and corruption, there’s a place for you on this campaign,” Ben McAdams, a former Democratic congressman from Utah and current candidate for the House, declared in a July 2026 Instagram post .

So talking about corruption is a way to talk about Trump and the Trump administration without mentioning them directly. Voters unhappy with Trump will assume corruption talk is an indictment of Trump, while Trump supporters may assume the corruption is elsewhere – after all, Trump won the 2016 election, in part, by promising to take on the corrupt establishment .
These distinctions – real corruption vs. corruption talk – go back at least to the country’s founding, if not beyond. Historically, corruption talk has stood in for other things.

For instance, the Progressive Era of the late 19th and early 20th centuries , a time when activists in both parties worked together to pursue reforms in government, economic policy and social policy, was the era in which we find that corruption talk was most prevalent in American politicians’ rhetoric. It was also a moment when America was almost as polarized and economically unequal as it is today , and many Americans saw this inequality as a symptom of corruption.

None of this is to deny that the U.S. currently has a president who has engaged in more overt acts of corruption than any other. Trump’s actions – from his family’s documented cryptocurrency profiteering to his appointment of a Cabinet full of conflicts of interest (such as stock ownership in companies regulated by their agencies, or a history of lobbying the very agencies they now run), to his alleged ties to the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein – no doubt have catalyzed this discussion.
Yet it is perhaps fitting that the nation’s 250th anniversary has been characterized by a return to a classic American preoccupation: the traditional American pastime of corruption talk.

Robert Boatright does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: In taking Syria off state sponsor of terrorism list, US is putting its faith in al-Qaida alumni – that presents risks and opportunities
articles.author:
<name>Jason M. Blazakis, Professor of the Practice and Director of Center on Terrorism, Extremism and Counterterrorism, Middlebury College</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jason-m-blazakis-1154151"/>
paras: Syria’s delisting as a state sponsor of terrorism was a long time coming.
The country had, after all, been on the U.S. State Department list of proscribed nations since it was created in 1979 – the only nation originally listed still on it.
That was until Aug. 24, 2026, when U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio formally rescinded Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism.
The shift removes barriers to American investment in Syria. But for the U.S. administration, it is also a bet on an unlikely figure.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa was a designated terrorist until November 2025 – it was my office within the State Department that designated him in May 2013 under the name Muhammad al-Jawlani .
In delisting Syria, the U.S. administration is wagering that the former Islamist militant has changed and can work with the U.S. in areas of foreign policy, economics and even possibly defense.

When the State Department created the state sponsor of terrorism list in December 1979 under the Export Administration Act, Syria joined fellow Middle Eastern countries Libya, Iraq and South Yemen on it.

By then, longtime Syrian leader Hafez al-Assad had turned Damascus into a headquarters for the Palestinian groups that opposed any negotiated settlement with Israel. The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine General Command, the Abu Nidal Organization and Palestinian Islamic Jihad all operated from Syrian soil, and Hamas kept its external leadership in Damascus until 2012.

Syria was also the land bridge for Iranian weapons bound for Hezbollah in Lebanon. When I ran the State Department’s Office of Counterterrorism Finance and Designations from 2008 to 2018, Syria appeared in every annual Country Reports on Terrorism, and the entry rarely changed.

The Syrian civil war that began during that period eventually saw the demise of the Assad regime – Hafez’s son Bashar had continued his father’s hard-line legacy after coming to power in 2000. But it also saw the rise of al-Sharaa as head of the Nusra Front, al-Qaida’s Syrian branch. Islamic State group founder Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi tasked al-Sharaa with building a beachhead in Syria for the terrorism network.

But when al-Baghdadi announced in April 2013 that the Nusra Front would be folded into the Islamic State group, al-Sharaa refused and pledged allegiance to al-Qaida’s Ayman al-Zawahiri instead. He then broke with al-Qaida in 2016.
Ten years on, al-Sharaa was received at the White House as a head of state, and the State Department removed him from the terrorist list.

The U.S. bet extends beyond one man. Syria’s security services were built from Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham, the successor group to the Nusra Front that al-Sharaa led to power in Syria. Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham was delisted by Rubio on the same day as Syria’s rescission.
Likewise, Syrian Interior Minister Anas Khattab , who was a founding member of the Nusra Front, was delisted as a global terrorist on the same day as al-Sharaa.

The International Crisis Group estimates that some 5,000 foreign fighters remain under arms inside state forces. And the Soufan Center warned in January that hard-liners within those services could break ranks and join the Islamic State group or other jihadist organizations. The Combating Terrorism Center at West Point reports that veteran foreign jihadists now openly call al-Sharaa a sellout.

In short, al-Qaida’s alumni are not adjacent to the Syrian state – they are inside it. The Trump administration is betting that working with that grouping is worth the risk. Yet critics fear the consequences for the U.S. of allying with a Syria with such a high prevalence of former militants.
Another important implication is that once a country is removed from the State Department list, getting it back on is bureaucratically cumbersome.

It requires the secretary of state finding that a government has repeatedly provided support for acts of international terrorism. “Repeatedly” is the operative word. In my experience a designation needs a documented pattern, an intelligence record that survives interagency review, and a decision at the top of the government. Even on the quickest timelines, like for Cuba in 2021 , it is a cumbersome process. And until that designation were to go back into effect, sanctions relief would keep flowing.

Supporters of delisting, however, have a reasonable geostrategic argument to make. The Assad family tied Syria to Moscow for half a century – bases at Tartus and Khmeimim gave the Kremlin its only military footprint on the Mediterranean.

A Syrian government that is friendly with the West and accepts American security assistance has less reason to lean on Russia. And every step Damascus takes toward Washington is a step away from Moscow.

Yet, the Trump administration cashed in Washington’s best chip with Syria’s removal from the state sponsor of terrorism list. Russia, for the time being, still has boots on the ground in Syria , and al-Sharaa visited Vladimir Putin in October 2025 .
If the Trump administration had waited until the end of 2026 to remove Syria from the state sponsor of terrorism list, it could have ensured that Russia vacated the military bases in Syria first.
But the U.S. president is keen to rush Syria into becoming an ally to Washington, not least because it would further isolate Iran, denying Tehran the influence it had under the Assad regime.

The Trump adminsistration’s policy shift could also have major domestic repercussions. Trump has been photographed with al-Sharaa in Riyadh and in the Oval Office. Those images are an asset while Syria adheres to Washington’s wishes. But they are a liability the moment it does not.

And the record already holds warnings. Government-aligned forces killed Alawite civilians on the Syrian coast in March 2025 and Druze civilians in Suwayda in July 2025 . These were abuses of state power under al-Sharaa’s authority.

For Syria, the calculus is mostly positive. The State Department’s prior designation carried a ban on defense exports, controls on dual-use goods, limits on foreign assistance, and financial restrictions that made international banks treat Syria as untouchable.
Comprehensive sanctions ended in June 2025; the designation was the last major legal barrier to American investment.

The delisting also opens the door to a counterterrorism partnership. Syria joined the coalition against the Islamic State group in November 2025 and has run operations against the terrorist group, al-Qaida and Hezbollah networks.

Al-Sharaa’s past with the Islamic State group is the reason he wants it destroyed; the group spent years trying to kill him after the 2013 split . His hatred of the Islamic State group appears genuine, and American cooperation with Damascus against the terrorist network will benefit the Syrians who suffered most under its rule.

One further consequence deserves consideration. Syria is the first state to leave the list after a once-designated terrorist replaced a designated regime. Other individuals classified as terrorists by the U.S. might well notice that the road from the list to the Oval Office can be short – and rewarding.
Jason M. Blazakis is running as a Democrat for Hunterdon County Commissioner.

articles.title: Seattle shapes Central District Black Legacy Plan to honor local history across neighborhood parks
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Powell Barnett being shown park development plans in October 1970 (Image: Seattle Municipal Archives)

Seattle Parks and Recreation is advancing a new capital initiative aimed at honoring the Central District’s pivotal Black activists, entrepreneurs, and philanthropists through improvements to neighborhood open spaces.

Dubbed the Central District Black Legacy Plan , the effort will fund site analysis, community engagement, and prioritized capital investments to transform selected Central District public grounds into spaces of remembrance and cultural celebration.
The initial phase focuses on three key neighborhood parks named after prominent Black historical figures:
If funding allows, the city plans to add up to two additional neighborhood locations to the project scope.

The city is currently seeking consultant teams to guide the initial planning and community-driven visioning phase, which will lay the groundwork for subsequent design development and construction. Seattle Parks and Recreation has placed a strong emphasis on community participation, actively encouraging proposals from first-time applicants and members of the Central District’s Black community to help shape the public spaces.

Meanwhile, construction is underway on the more than $11 million Garfield Super Block renovation, bringing a long-championed community vision to life at the Central District campus. Led by the Garfield Super Block Coalition in partnership with the city, the project reimagines the grounds surrounding Garfield High School and community center with a 0.34-mile “Legacy and Promise Promenade” celebrating the area’s rich multicultural history through public art, alongside upgraded multi-use sports courts, a new restroom facility, and the city’s first dedicated public parkour park.

Crews have already completed the synthetic turf infield at Playfield G1, installed key play equipment, and poured the southeast accessibility ramp, with pathway improvements advancing through the fall and a full project completion expected in early 2027.

While Seattle Parks and Recreation has not published an exact dollar figure for the Central District Black Legacy Plan, the initiative is supported by the Seattle Park District’s Park CommUNITY Fund .

For a municipal project of this scope, the initial 12- to 18-month planning and community engagement phase typically commands a consultant contract in the $150,000 to $350,000 range. Once planning is complete, the physical capital improvements, spanning interpretive art, landscape redesign, and infrastructure across three to five neighborhood parks, are likely to require an estimated $1 million to $4+ million in construction funding.

According to historical U.S. Census Bureau records and municipal housing analyses, the Central District’s Black population peaked around 1970 at roughly 70% to 73% neighborhood-wide, reaching nearly 90% in its most concentrated core tracts due to decades of redlining. Recent U.S. Census American Community Survey data and City of Seattle demographic reports show that share has dropped to approximately 10% to 14% today, driven by decades of gentrification, rising housing costs, and regional displacement.

articles.title: Bellevue Permitting More New Housing Than Seattle, Intake Data Shows
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: More applications for new homes were submitted over the first six months of the year in Bellevue than across the lake in Seattle, according to preliminary permit activity data reported by both cities. In Bellevue, new permit applications were submitted for at least 1,585 new multifamily units between January and June, compared to just 1,137 new units in Seattle.
The imbalance is quite the turnaround for Seattle's once red-hot development market, now getting lapped by a city with one-fifth of its population.

Bellevue's impressive numbers are a testament to the work that civic leaders in the Eastside's largest job center have been doing in recent years to open the doors to housing growth, especially in areas near light rail like Downtown, Wilburton, and BelRed.

Getting surpassed by Bellevue could be setting off alarm bells at Seattle City Hall. Mayor Katie Wilson campaigned to victory last year on a platform of affordable and abundant housing, pledging to ramp up homebuilding.

With new housing unit applications in Seattle on track to see a 30% decline in 2026 after already dropping 38% in 2025, the Emerald City faces a development slump that will likely have a significant impact on rents in the coming years. This is especially true if the pace of new residential buildings opening their doors continues to slow to a crawl.
Thanks to the bounty of permits approved in the early 2020s, Seattle still managed to bring more than 8,000 homes online in 2025, but with permit intake plummeting, eventually the well will go dry.

The initial data on new permit applications in both cities are preliminary, with applications not required to include unit counts at the intake stage. That means the total number of units being submitted in new permit applications in Bellevue is actually even higher than the 1,585 number – but it's unclear by how much.

"Based on applications for projects that developers did choose to provide unit counts, multifamily permit applications reflect at least 1,585 proposed units; however, that is a partial number because there are a handful of multifamily projects that did not provide unit counts," Amanda Rich Anderson, a Development Services spokesperson, told The Urbanist . "The true total is higher, but I don’t know how much higher."
Likewise, Seattle's 1,137 units may also be an undercount, with firmer numbers only released when permits are issued.

It's likely that Bellevue may have even lapped Seattle on the metric of new units entering the pipeline sometime last year, with Bellevue's overall development activity reaching new heights in 2025. According to data presented to the Bellevue City Council last month, residents and builders applied for more than 18,000 permits of all types last year – including commercial permits and renovations – with planners expecting that trend to continue through 2026.

One of Bellevue's biggest hotspots is Wilburton, an area currently dominated by car dealerships and surface parking lots, but which the city rezoned early last year in hopes of seeing just such a development boom. Located just across the I-405 chasm from downtown, Wilburton benefits from a light rail station that opened in 2024, with 2 Line service extended across the lake to Seattle this March.

Within the neighborhood's boundaries, developers are able to take advantage of a program that has been dubbed the "Wilburton Supercharger." The Supercharger allows builders to "double count" affordable units provided under the state's Multifamily Tax Exemption (MFTE) program and a city-mandated affordable housing requirement together, offsetting the mandate to provide below market-rate units with a tax break.

"In plain English, it looks like this: In exchange for setting aside 20% of a project as affordable to households earning up to 80% of area median income — roughly $80,000 a year for a family of two — a developer receives a 12-year property tax exemption on the residential improvements," said Bellevue Chamber of Commerce President Joe Fain in an op-ed in The Urbanist earlier this year. "For projects where on-site units aren’t the best fit, there is a fee-in-lieu option that still funds affordability elsewhere in the city."

Bellevue boosters including Fain have pointed to the Supercharger as an example that the rest of the region should follow, backing up their affordable housing mandates with real incentives for developers. Earlier this year the Bellevue Council approved a temporary expansion of the supercharger into other commercial districts around the city, with the exception of Downtown Bellevue. That temporary expansion occurred over the recommendation of city staff, and after intense negotiations with affordable housing advocates who were wary of giving up requirements for developers to build more deeply affordable units.
The picture around affordable housing mandates is very different in Seattle.

While tweaks to Seattle's MFTE program approved last year were intended to make the program more palatable for developers, the city's Mandatory Housing Affordability (MHA) program requires much deeper levels of affordability typically ranging between 5% and 10% or for developers to pay a hefty fee. When facing economic headwinds like Seattle is right now, the added fees contribute to projects not being feasible and not getting off the ground.

Other than automatic inflationary increases, MHA fees haven't been recalibrated for years, and a group called the Seattle Housing Roundtable – echoing the name of a similar group that got the Wilburton Supercharger across the finish line, the Eastside Housing Roundtable – has been pushing for a temporary break on MHA fees to get stalled projects moving. The backlog of stalled projects is extensive; the roundtable estimates that builders are essentially sitting on at least 70 shovel-ready proposals encompassing 8,000 homes, hoping for more favorable economic conditions and investor interest.

So far, calls to cut fees haven't been heeded at city hall. Wilson punted action on MHA fees to next year, after losing support from key affordable housing providers and pledging more stakeholder work. Instead, Wilson issued an executive order this month aimed at streamline permitting, while launching a broader "Housing Production Task Force " to key in on deeper reforms. The order also proposes a new city-funded "affordable housing ombuds" that will help developers navigate the city's convoluted processes.

"We want housing opportunities across every neighborhood in our city, so that the size of your paycheck doesn't determine your zip code, your access to healthy air, or the safety of your streets," Wilson said at her task force announcement. "That means more market-rate housing to keep pace with our city's growth. It means affordable housing that people working every kind of job can afford, with homes large enough for every kind of family. And it means housing for our retirees and for those who can no longer or are unable to work. It means social housing that provides a stable, affordable, mixed-income place to live as a household's income changes, and it means supportive housing paired with services so we can get people the care they need."

Wilson shared a hope that permit streamlining alone could jumpstart housing production, but the Seattle Housing Roundtable has argued that cutting fees will be necessary to spur projects, not just faster permits. Builders have also flagged excessive utility hookup fees as a growing issue.

"First, we are taking more aggressive and coordinated action to make permitting faster and clearer," Wilson said. "That begins with looking closely at our own regulatory and permitting processes, building on work begun during the previous administration and championed by advocates, developers, councilmembers, and City staff, we are launching a new residential permitting interdepartmental team to make permit timelines shorter and more predictable across the city. As the developers gathered here today know too well, delayed permitting, utility hookups, and street-use permits can cost a single project hundreds of thousands of dollars per month of delay."

The debate about permitting and fees happening against the backdrop of a stalled citywide zoning update as part of Seattle's Comprehensive Plan, with modest zoning changes now pushed into 2027 due to legal appeals from homeowner groups. Wilson plans to go above and beyond the changes proposed by her predecessor Bruce Harrell. Her proposal, dubbed the " Taller Denser Faster " plan, remains in early stages, though it may be helped down the line by a new law limiting how those types of appeals can be filed.
If Seattle is going to attempt a Hail Mary that could reverse the decline in permits coming in the door, it likely can't sit by and wait for those zoning changes to come down the pike.

Meanwhile, Bellevue is heading toward further rezones and zoning tweaks intended to spur housing, eyeing changes to the BelRed neighborhood as well as Downtown, as part of a broader " Downtown Livability 2.0 " code amendment process. Combined with the recently adopted Housing Opportunities in Mixed-Use Areas code update, which brought the Supercharger to new places in the city, the City expects the building boom to continue.

"[I]ncreases in housing production are likely to come in the future based on recent policy changes and code updates that focused on housing and that is not going to be captured by the 2026 data for building permits," Rich Anderson wrote.
At a certain point, Seattle might need to start looking across the lake for ideas and a sense of urgency, or risk falling even further behind.

articles.title: Democrats Poised to Gain Seats in Washington State Legislature
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Primary results finalized last week make clear that Washington State Democrats are on track to pick up seats in the state legislature this fall. The most dramatic flips are queued up in Clark County, where the 17th and 18th Legislative Districts are currently held by Republicans. Democrats are now heavily favored to win those House seats after a strong showing in the primary.

Democrats already flipped the 18th's state senate seat in 2024, putting Adrian Cortes into office. Democrats are now well-positioned to unseat the district's two Republican state House members, who are well below the 50% mark in the primary and extremely vulnerable.

Even the 14th LD (Yakima Valley) and 25th Legislative District (Greater Puyallup), which have both long been Republican strongholds, are looking to be in play after Republicans barely cleared the 50% bar. The 25th represents the last district in the Seattle-Tacoma metropolitan area still held by Republicans after a decade of steady losses . With 50.2% of the primary vote, incumbent Michael Keaton is holding on for dear life, and will face school board director David Berg .

In swing districts where Republicans have hoped to erase recent losses, 2026 primary voters gave them no quarter. The 42nd LD (Whatcom County) continues to trend toward Democrats. Incumbent Rep. Alicia Rule grabbed 56% of the vote in Position 1, and incumbent Rep. Joe Timmons pulled in 54% in Position 2.

The same is true in the swingy 26th Legislative District, covering Kitsap County. Democrats won the most votes in all three races, led by state senator Deborah Krishnadasan's 56% share in her reelection bid. The Position 2 seat, meanwhile, is set to be a pickup for Democrats. Republican Rep. Michelle Caldier's retirement erased incumbency advantage in the race.

Democratic candidate Renee Hernandez Greenfield (who won the endorsement of the The Urbanist Elections Committee, on which I serve) will face Republican primary winner Katy Cornell, who mustered 44.7% of the vote. Hernandez Greenfield will likely complete the sweep of 26th for Democrats.

The lack of Republican momentum in Washington State pours cold water on the theory that a conservative backlash is brewing due to the passage of progressive legislation, such as the millionaires' tax or carbon pricing in the Climate Commitment Act , moves which Republican leaders and conservative-leaning pundits have framed as oversteps. In fact, Democrats only continue to gain.

State democrats already secured a supermajority, winning more than 60% of seats in 2024 , but that majority is on course to grow. If they flip two house seats in 17th and 18th and the take last Republican holdout in the 26th, that would be a gain of five House seats. Democrats' 59-39 advantage in the house would grow to 64-34, a 30-seat edge.

If the 14th and 25th LDs come into play, the margin would be even greater. With the Trump brand so toxic in Washington state and Republicans in full-blown political collapse mode, it's certainly possible.

The 17th LD currently has a Republican trifecta. State Senator Paul Harris narrowly fended off a Democratic challenger in 2024, winning 51% of the vote. He'll survive 2026 only by the fact he's not up for reelection until 2028.

Clark County is one of the fastest-growing areas of the state, but it's also long been relatively conservative, seen as a low-tax safety value for the Portland metropolitan area and a magnet for retirees. Washington has no income tax (the millionaires' tax won't kick in until 2029 and all but the richest will be exempt) and Oregon has no sales tax; Clark County residents get the best of both worlds if they drive across the border to shop.

While the 49th LD, which spans the county seat of Vancouver, has been held by Democrats, the rest of the more sprawling Clark County exurbs have traditionally been fertile ground for Republicans. That appears on the cusp of changing.

Democrats didn't just eke out a narrow win in the primary; they dominated. Incumbent Republican Rep. Paul Stuebe managed to win just 45% of the vote. He appears set to lose to Diane Perez , who won 55%. Double digit losses for incumbents are rare, but Stuebe found a way.

Incumbent Rep. Kevin Waters did even worse, winning just 43.9% of the vote. Democratic challenger Ben Christly won 52.3% and is the clear frontrunner. It's a shocking fall for an incumbent that did not even face a challenger in 2024 and coasted to victory running unopposed.

In the 18th LD, Democratic challenger Randi Knott is leading incumbent Rep. Stephanie McClintock 52% to 48%. In the Position 2 race, union organizer Deken Letinich is leading incumbent Rep. John Ley 53% to 46%.

Even an open seat state senate seat was tough sledding for the Republican candidate, Erika Creydt, who managed to win just 44.5% of the vote against two Democrats and an independent. Incumbent Sharon Shewmake, somewhat of an urbanist celebrity who is known to hand out bicycle pins to allies around Olympia, declined to seek an additional term.

The Democrat who made it through in the 42nd is not yet official. Michael Alvarez Shepard edged out Eamonn Collins by just four votes, a margin so close it triggered a hand recount , which started Tuesday and is expected to be completed by Friday.

Flipping Republican seats isn't the only way that the state Democratic caucus will change. The 2026 primary also saw a good number of progressive candidates challenging more centrist or establishment Democrats.

Educator Kelabe Tewolde fared the best of the lefties challenging incumbents, winning 51.5% of the vote to 47.8% for 28-year incumbent Sharon Tomiko Santos. Tewolde secured a number of high-profile endorsements, including from King County Executive Girmay Zahilay, Seattle Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck, The Stranger, and The Urbanist.

Redmond City Councilmember Jessica Forsythe also has a strong chance of unseating incumbent Rep. Amy Walen in the 48th LD. Forsythe narrowly edged Walen in the primary by 17 votes. It's sure to be one of the most expensive state legislature races this fall, with wealthy backers likely to flood support for Walen, who drew the ire of progressives for voting against the millionaires' tax and statewide middle housing reform. Just two years ago, big money poured in to help Walen get elected to the Senate, a bid that fell flat with voters sticking with incumbent Vandana Slatter.

Forsythe's endorsements include The Urbanist , King County Democrats, the Washington State Labor Council, WA Bikes, Sierra Club, former Governor Jay Inslee, and (perhaps not surprisingly) Senator Slatter.

Likewise, former Tacoma Council candidate Krista Perez emerged from the primary leading incumbent Rep. Melanie Morgan in the 29th LD. Endorsed by The Urbanist, Perez is 2.3 points ahead of Morgan, who has just 46% of the vote, but Perez's victory was muted by a DUI arrest this month , which could well be a drag on her chances in the general – especially in light from some cringeworthy comments from her lawyer, seeking to paint drunk driving crashes as no big deal.

In the 46th LD, long-time Rep. Gerry Pollet, who has often been a thorn in the side of urbanists on housing reforms, is fending off a progressive challenge. Pollet mustered 51.6% of the vote so he remains favored as he squares off with Will Dreher in the primary. A litigator promising reforms to AI policy, Dreher earned The Stranger's endorsement, which propelled him to victory over Urbanist-backed Ron Davis , who ran to the left of both. After getting knocked out in the primary, Davis continued to portray Dreher as a fake progressive and voiced support for Pollet, posting a screed on his website implying The Stranger's ownership group had intervened and blocked him from being endorsed, which the union representing the Stranger's staff has refuted . Even with Davis nipping at his heels, Dreher might still have a shot to close the gap.

In the 43rd LD, the bid from labor leader Hannah Sabio-Howell to unseat Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen looks to be ill-fated after Pedersen won two-thirds of the primary vote. A former chair of The Urbanist Elections Committee, Sabio-Howell had a number of progressive endorsements (including from The Urbanist , State Rep. Shaun Scott, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, and Councilmember Rinck). However, it was not enough to erase Pedersen's incumbency advantage, especially with him fresh off of passing the millionaires' tax , which he spearheaded as lead sponsor. The Stranger endorsed Pedersen, likely sapping progressive support from Sabio-Howell.

While Sabio-Howell supporters may find her result disappointing, Washington Community Alliance executive director Kamau Chege (who is also Sabio-Howell's spouse) argued in an op-ed in The Urbanist that progressive challenges are steadily defining the party and pulling it out its centrist rut, even if some particular candidates come up short. Perhaps, Pedersen never would have become an enthusiastic backer of the millionaires tax or rent stabilization if not for the credible threat of a progressive coming for his seat.
Whatever the particular reasons for shifts in each race, the 2027 state legislature is poised to be the progressive in Washington history.

articles.title: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson Signs Order on Traffic Safety
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: Last week Seattle politicians spent a whole lot of time talking about public safety, but one actually did something about it.

The big news came on Friday when Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson signed an executive order on Vision Zero, the city’s goal to reduce traffic fatalities and serious injuries to zero by 2030. Numbers have been trending the wrong way for years—19 pedestrians died on the city’s streets in 2025, compared to six in 2016.

Safe street advocates have said the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) has been too slow to install barrier-protected bike lanes and narrow roads to discourage speeding. They also say SDOT has historically favored drivers’ concerns, like preserving on-street parking, over reducing collisions.

Wilson’s executive order aims to rebalance the department’s priorities. It directs SDOT to move several planned safety projects to the top of the queue and make more short-term improvements on dangerous arterials. The executive order also directs city-owned vehicles to be retrofitted with better mirrors and side guards , authorizes up to 10 new automated speed cameras, and instructs the City’s lobbyists to advocate for traffic safety laws in Olympia.

But as with anything related to City Hall, the Vision Zero announcement couldn’t go ahead without a lot of gesturing, grandstanding, and political point scoring. Last week’s culprits: Councilmembers Rob Saka and Bob Kettle.
Days before Wilson’s signing ceremony, Councilmember Rob Saka proposed his own safety legislation, the “SAFER Streets Act.”

It’s so similar to Wilson’s order—both call for truck side guards, ask for infrastructure improvements like intersection daylighting , and assign SDOT’s chief traffic engineer to oversee traffic safety—that it is unclear why he introduced it in the first place. The Vision Zero order wasn’t a surprise. Wilson and Seattle City Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck had been working on it for months. Another wrinkle: he did not formally introduce the bill during Thursday’s Transportation, Waterfront, and Seattle Center Committee meeting he chairs. Instead, Saka added it as an informational item onto the agenda because it was incomplete. He still has not officially introduced the legislation. Saka did not attend Wilson’s signing ceremony with Rinck and Councilmember Eddie Lin. When asked about this, Wilson said, “we’re going to work together, and I’m excited about his leadership too.”

“Public safety” talk is in the air. Wilson’s Vision Zero order, and Saka’s rush job, come amid a month-long media cycle over public safety and gun violence following the tragic Seattle Center shooting . (In an attempt to reframe the conversation at the press conference, Wilson said, “traffic safety is part of public safety.”)

But an August 20 opinion poll commissioned by the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce once again brought public safety to the top of the news agenda. Carried out by the firm Fulcrum Strategy Group, it showed a dramatic 46 percent decline in Wilson’s approval ratings since April. Only one third of the 500 respondents said they were confident in Wilson’s public safety plan, while the City Council also received a dismal -16 percent approval rating.

Councilmember Bob Kettle seized upon the poll with a Friday morning press conference during which he said the words “public safety” 45 times in 50 minutes. He criticized Wilson’s delayed Bite of Seattle shooting press conference and commended the response from police department officers as “textbook.”

Not everyone viewed the SPD response as positively. Multiple armed police officers were present in the vicinity of the shooting, suggesting their presence did not deter the violence. The department did not use its emergency text alert service, leading some Bite of Seattle attendees to resort to calling 911 for guidance . A month later, one of the shooting suspects remains at large.

At Wilson’s request, the Seattle Office of Inspector General for Public Safety is investigating the City’s response. Kettle urged the office to include Wilson and her staff in its report. While he was at it, Kettle once again lambasted Wilson for pausing the expansion of the Seattle Police Department’s CCTV surveillance program. The corporate media audience—the Seattle Times , the four TV news stations and conservative-leaning Center Square—dutifully bought into the framing, despite the lack of any substantive announcements.
Kettle did not address traffic safety or Vision Zero, topics he said were outside the remit of the Public Safety Committee he chairs.

Last year’s annual public safety survey from Seattle University showed more than 45 percent of nearly 9,000 respondents listed traffic safety as their top concern; data from the Washington State Traffic Safety Commission and the SPD suggests both traffic fatalities and serious violent crime present serious hazards to the public. Between 2016 and 2025, 443 people died by homicide in Seattle, whereas 328 people died in traffic-related accidents. For every four homicides in that period, three people died during road collisions, nearly half of them pedestrians. With last year’s dip in homicides, the numbers reached near-parity.

For safe street advocates like Seattle Streets Alliance executive director Gordon Padelford, Wilson’s Vision Zero order gives hope that traffic safety will no longer be relegated to the bottom of the City’s political agenda.
“We’ve just gotten so numb to death and serious injuries on our streets that sometimes people forget about it,” he says. “They just think it’s inevitable.”
